source.text: Uisang, verses of the Diagram of the Dharma Realm of the One Vehicle of Hwaeom (30 lines of 7 characters, 210 characters)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

b01.plain: The Dharma nature is perfectly interfused, with no two aspects; all dharmas are unmoving, originally still.
b01.commentary: The first line of the ode is also its conclusion. The true nature of all things (the Dharma nature) is undivided, and everything blends together without obstruction (perfect interfusion).

b02.plain: Without name or form, cut off from everything, it is known only by the wisdom of awakening, not by any other realm.
b02.commentary: The Dharma nature cannot be grasped by words or thought; it is known only by the wisdom of realization.

b03.plain: The true nature is very deep and utterly subtle; it does not hold to a self-nature but comes into being according to conditions.
b03.commentary: Because it has no fixed self-nature (emptiness), it can appear in every form according to conditions. This is the Hwaeom (Avataṃsaka) view of dependent origination.

b04.plain: In one is all, in many is one; one is all, many is one.
b04.commentary: The best-known line of the ode. It holds the Hwaeom teachings of mutual containment and mutual identity in a single line.

b05.plain: A single mote of dust contains the ten directions, and so does every mote of dust.
b05.commentary: The largest is contained in the smallest. This is the Hwaeom worldview, beyond big and small in space.

b06.plain: Measureless distant kalpas are a single thought; a single thought is measureless kalpas.
b06.commentary: If the previous line is about space, this one is about time. An instant and eternity do not obstruct each other.

b07.plain: The nine times and the ten times are identical with one another, yet without confusion each stands distinct.
b07.commentary: The nine times are past, present and future, each with its own past, present and future; the ten times add the single thought that embraces them all.

b08.plain: The moment one first arouses the mind is right awakening; birth-and-death and nirvana are always in harmony.
b08.commentary: "The first arousal of the mind is right awakening" comes from the Avataṃsaka Sutra and means that the beginning and end of practice are not two. It also appears in the Verse Summary of the Avataṃsaka.

b09.plain: Principle and phenomena merge in profound oneness, without distinction; this is the realm of the ten Buddhas and of great beings like Samantabhadra.
b09.commentary: Principle is the essence; phenomena are appearances. Their unobstructed oneness is the heart of Hwaeom.

b10.plain: Within the Buddha's ocean-seal samādhi, inconceivable wonders pour forth at will without end.
b10.commentary: "The Capable and Kind" (Neungin) translates the name Śākyamuni. The ocean-seal samādhi is a meditation that reflects everything, as a calm sea reflects all things.

b11.plain: A rain of jewels benefiting beings fills all of space; each being receives benefit according to the size of their vessel.
b11.commentary: The teaching falls on all without distinction, but what each receives depends on the vessel (capacity) of the one receiving.

b12.plain: Therefore, for the practitioner to return to the original source, it can never be done without stilling deluded thoughts.
b12.commentary: From here the ode speaks of the path of practice. The original source is the Dharma nature.

b13.plain: With unconditioned, skillful means, grasp the wish-fulfilling jewel; returning home, gain provisions according to your share.
b13.commentary: Home stands for the original place; provisions for the merit and wisdom needed on the way.

b14.plain: With the inexhaustible treasure of dhāraṇī, adorn the true jewel palace of the Dharma realm.
b14.commentary: Dhāraṇī is the power to gather and hold all merit. With it the whole Dharma realm is adorned.

b15.plain: At last one sits on the seat of the Middle Way, in the true place; what has never moved from of old is called Buddha.
b15.commentary: The last line of the ode. One does not newly become a Buddha; one only confirms the place that never moved. It echoes the opening line, "all dharmas are unmoving, originally still."

beopseong.definition: The true nature of all things (dharmas). Used in the same sense as suchness or true reality.
